case_study_insert.main_stem: Marden Industrial Pumpworks (MIPW) is a private limited company in the industrial machinery sector, manufacturing precision pumps for water-treatment plants and supplying municipal contracts across two regions, with a workforce of 60. Founded in 2007 by Anja Marden, it operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. MIPW plans to invest $720,000 in a CNC machining cell for pump impellers, financed by a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and $270,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $360,000 a year, a variable cost of $18.00 a unit and a selling price of $30.00, and produces 40,000 units a year. MIPW faces a 5.5% defect rate on impeller castings and rising scrap levels that threaten distributor deliveries under tight customer windows.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Log — Q4 2025: The impeller line inspected 9,800 units last quarter at a defect rate of 5.5%, down from 7.2% a year earlier. Customer complaints fell from 41 to 26 per month. Average supplier lead time is 21 days. Market research of 500 water-treatment buyers found that 68% would pay up to $0.90 more for certified precision impellers, and 57% check supplier quality records before ordering. Rework on defective castings cost $6,800 last quarter.

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.00%, increasing variable-rate loan costs. (2) The national minimum wage rose 5.8% to $14.60 per hour from April 2026. (3) Steel and cast-iron input prices rose 9.6% year-on-year while industrial machinery price inflation ran at 6.3% and business confidence fell 2.1 points.

questions.question_text: MIPW plans to fund part of its CNC machining cell with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for MIPW of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using the $270,000 retained profit costs MIPW no interest or scheduled repayments, protecting cash flow while the business already carries fixed costs of $360,000 a year and a $450,000 bank loan. Every dollar saved can absorb the 9.6% rise in steel and cast-iron input costs, helping Anja Marden keep the $30.00 selling price competitive on municipal water-treatment contracts without borrowing more.

Point 2: Retained profit does not require collateral or give a lender power to repossess the new CNC cell if demand slips, so the $720,000 investment is safer. It also preserves the existing owners' control: no bank can impose conditions on how the 60-worker site is run, which matters when a 5.5% defect rate is already straining output and management needs freedom to re organise production quickly.

For a firm of 60 employees producing 40,000 units, the choice also affects risk: retained profit is internal and already earned, so it cannot be withdrawn by a lender if the 5.5% defect rate pushes rework above the $6,800 spent last quarter. Founder Anja Marden keeps control of the $720,000 cell and can redirect the $270,000 if municipal orders slip. By contrast, servicing the $450,000 loan on top of $360,000 fixed costs would consume contribution from the 30,000 units needed to break even, so internal funding protects the 10,000-unit margin of safety.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to the named business.

questions.question_text: MIPW is launching a new certified precision impeller range. Consider advertising in trade journals, sponsoring a water-industry exhibition, or direct technical sales visits. Which should MIPW choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Trade journal advertising: Print and online trade journals reach precisely the municipal and water-treatment engineers who buy precision impellers, and they are relatively cheap for a 60-employee firm. The drawback is that a static advert cannot demonstrate machining accuracy, and readership is narrow, so it may not generate the volume needed to justify the $720,000 CNC cell.

Industry exhibition sponsorship: A water-industry exhibition lets MIPW show sample impellers and meet buyers face to face, building credibility for certified quality and directly addressing the 57% of surveyed buyers who check supplier records. However, stand and sponsorship costs are high, and with a 5.5% defect rate the sales team would be demonstrating a product whose quality is still variable.

Direct technical sales visits: Engineers can visit plants, inspect tolerance data and discuss the $0.90 premium that 68% of surveyed buyers accept, giving high-quality leads and immediate feedback on the 9,800-unit inspection results. Reach is slow and travel costs mount, but each visit targets a genuine prospective contract.

All three routes must be judged against the 10,000-unit margin of safety and the $12.00 contribution: the launch pays only if enough of the 500 surveyed buyers convert. Technical visits give engineers the certification evidence behind the 68% premium acceptance, and results from the 9,800 inspected units can be shown directly. A campaign that merely builds awareness would not fix the 5.5% defect rate that caused 26 monthly complaints, so spending on broad reach before quality is consistent would waste cash needed for the $450,000 loan.

Recommendation: MIPW should choose direct technical sales visits, supported by short trade-journal adverts. They convert the 68% acceptance of a premium into orders and demonstrate quality personally. Exhibition sponsorship is rejected as too expensive and risky while the defect rate is unresolved; journals alone are rejected as too passive to sell a precision component.

questions.question_text: MIPW's hierarchical structure and autocratic leadership coincide with a 5.5% defect rate on impeller castings. Explain two benefits for MIPW of adopting a more democratic leadership style with its workforce of 60.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership invites the 60 operators to suggest practical fixes on the CNC impeller line, so the people handling the castings daily can identify the causes of the 5.5% defect rate before scrap is produced. This directly supports the $720,000 investment, because a machine is only as good as the process suggestions of the team running it, and it reduces the $6,800 rework bill.

Point 2: Being consulted raises job satisfaction and commitment under Maslow's social and esteem needs, which can stabilise output of 40,000 units and protect the margin of safety. Anja Marden would replace top-down instructions with shared problem solving, cutting disputes under the hierarchical structure and helping MIPW honour the 21-day supplier lead time and the 26 monthly complaints target.

The link to productivity is clear: 40,000 units divided by 60 workers is 666.67 units per worker, so a small improvement in attendance or useful suggestions from the line adds output without extra fixed cost. Democratic consultation also helps MIPW honour the 21-day supplier lead time and reduce the 26 monthly complaints, protecting the $0.90 premium accepted by 68% of the 500 surveyed buyers.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to the named business.

questions.question_text: MIPW wants to cut its 5.5% defect rate. Consider final inspection (quality control) or prevention through quality assurance and operator training. Which should MIPW choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Final inspection (quality control): Checking finished impellers would catch defective castings before dispatch, protecting the 26-per-month complaint figure and the $30.00 price. It is simple to introduce and gives immediate data from the 9,800 units inspected. However, it detects waste after resources have been spent, leaving the $6,800 rework cost and the 7.2%-to-5.5% improvement hard to sustain, and it does not fix the cause.

Quality assurance and training: Preventing faults through agreed process checks and on-the-job operator training attacks the source of the 5.5% defect rate, so fewer of the 40,000 units need rework, protecting contribution of $12.00 a unit and the $720,000 CNC investment. It costs time and requires a culture change from autocratic leadership, and results appear more slowly than inspection.

Implementation should be measured: MIPW can drive the 5.5% rate lower (it has already fallen from 7.2%) and require the $6,800 rework bill to fall, with weekly review under the democratic style. Training must cover all 60 workers because the CNC cell changes every impeller setting; excluding one shift would leave a skills gap. The insert gives no course fees or training hours, so no exact cost or payback is asserted; the recommendation rests on attacking the source of the defect and protecting the 10,000-unit margin of safety at 40,000 units.

Decision: MIPW should choose prevention through quality assurance and operator training, retaining only light final sampling. It removes the $6,800 rework bill at source and protects the margin of safety. Pure inspection is rejected because it finds faults after the cost is incurred, and training alone without process checks would not give the consistent tolerances water-treatment buyers demand.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies relevant factors with limited application to the named business.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of both quality approaches with application to MIPW's defect rate and costs.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of inspection and prevention in context with a justified decision rejecting the alternative.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how MIPW's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $360,000 ÷ ($30.00 − $18.00) = $360,000 ÷ $12.00 = 30,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 30,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $30.00 − $18.00 = $12.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $12.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways MIPW's management can use this cost, break-even and productivity data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the break-even output of 30,000 units with actual production of 40,000 units, giving a margin of safety of 10,000 units, so they know how far demand can fall before MIPW makes a loss.
2. Contribution per unit of $12.00 shows what each unit adds towards fixed costs of $360,000; for illustration, a $1.00 price cut would reduce contribution to $11.00 and raise break-even to 32,727.27 units, letting managers test pricing before committing.
3. Average total cost of $27.00 a unit ($360,000 ÷ 40,000 units plus $18.00 variable cost) provides a benchmark each quarter to track the 5.5% defect rate on impeller castings and decide whether rework is pushing unit cost above plan.
4. Labour productivity of 666.67 units per worker (40,000 units ÷ workforce of 60) shows whether the $720,000 investment can be handled by the existing team, or whether recruitment is needed before the wage bill rises.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 30,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $12.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety against 40,000 units; illustrative pricing and the $360,000 fixed costs; the $720,000 investment decision; and unit-cost and productivity benchmarking to tackle the 5.5% defect rate on impeller castings.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate MIPW's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has MIPW's financial position improved? Which of the two ratios is the stronger evidence? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.40 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.60 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.80 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.00 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $120,000 inventories + $110,000 trade receivables + $50,000 cash = $280,000; 2025 current assets = $114,000 + $150,000 + $40,000 = $304,000. For 2024, $280,000 ÷ $200,000 = 1.40, and ($280,000 − $120,000) ÷ $200,000 = 0.80. For 2025, $304,000 ÷ $190,000 = 1.60, and ($304,000 − $114,000) ÷ $190,000 = 1.00. All source figures are the $'000 values in Appendix 2.

Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened on both measures, so MIPW's short-term financial position has improved. Current assets rose from $280,000 to $304,000 while current liabilities fell from $200,000 to $190, and receivables climbed from $110,000 to $150,000, so more cash is tied up with customers even though the $450,000 loan is being serviced.
The acid test ratio is the stronger evidence of real improvement because it rose from 0.80 to 1.00 without relying on inventories, which are the least liquid current asset.

These ratios are a snapshot at 31 March 2025 and the insert gives no sector average or longer trend, so one year of improvement cannot prove lasting strength. The $150,000 of trade receivables and $114,000 of inventories may prove slow to convert if impeller designs change, so the 1.40 and 1.60 figures should be read alongside the $720,000 commitment.

Conclusion: MIPW's financial position has improved: both liquidity measures are higher in 2025 and the gain survives the exclusion of inventories. Credit control should be tightened on the larger receivables balance before the next $720,000 commitment.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies relevant factors with limited application to the named business.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for both years with some contextual comment on the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years, detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities, an explicit answer on the stronger ratio, and a justified conclusion.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for MIPW of using automated CNC machining instead of manual machining for its impeller production.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Automated CNC machining can hold tighter tolerances than manual work, which directly attacks the 5.5% defect rate and the $6,800 rework bill, protecting the $12.00 contribution on each of 40,000 units and supporting the 68% of buyers who accept a $0.90 premium for certified precision. It also makes the $720,000 expansion viable against fixed costs of $360,000.

Disadvantage: CNC equipment adds substantial fixed costs and depends on the variable cost of $18.00 a unit staying stable; with steel input costs rising 9.6%, an automated line has less flexibility than skilled manual machinists if specifications change. It also needs new skills from the workforce of 60, so teething problems could initially worsen the 5.5% defect rate rather than improve it.

Managers should also note that automation changes the cost mix: the $720,000 raises fixed costs above the current $360,000, so break-even output of 30,000 units must still be covered while steel and cast-iron costs rise 9.6%. The insert gives no machine life, output gain or payback figure, so none is claimed; the decision rests on quality and capacity, not an invented saving. If the 5.5% defect rate were not reduced, the $6,800 rework bill would erode the $12.00 contribution on each of the 40,000 units.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to the named business.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.00%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase to $14.60 and the 9.6% rise in steel and cast-iron input costs will affect MIPW. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
MIPW faces three external changes reported in Appendix 3.

Base interest rate 4.25% to 5.00%: If the $450,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage-point rise adds 0.0075 × $450,000 ten-year bank loan = $3,375 a year (0.0075 × 450,000). That is modest beside fixed costs of $360,000 and the $720,000 investment, and a fixed-rate loan would avoid it completely, though future borrowing would cost more and customers may cut spending.

Minimum wage up 5.8% to $14.60: With a workforce of 60, this raises the wage bill on every production hour and cannot be avoided. The insert states neither hours worked nor individual pay rates, so no defensible annual total can be invented; against the given productivity of 666.67 units per worker, the rise is absorbable only if output per worker holds, otherwise unit labour cost rises and the $12.00 contribution per unit is squeezed.

9.6% steel and cast-iron input costs: The insert does not decompose the $18.00 variable cost per unit, so only a labelled upper-bound illustration is honest: if the entire $18.00 were exposed, the rise would add 0.096 × $18.00 = $1.728 a unit, or $69,120 a year at 40,000 units. Even the upper bound is smaller than the contribution lost if the 5.5% defect rate were not fixed, so quality and cost control must run together.

Conclusion: the 9.6% rise in steel and cast-iron input costs will have the greatest impact. It compounds on every one of the 40,000 units, directly erodes the $12.00 contribution that justifies the $720,000 plan, and dwarfs the $3,375 interest effect; the wage rise is material but cannot be quantified from the insert. Anja Marden should negotiate steel prices and use the $0.90 precision premium rather than relying on the modest interest saving.
